title.official: Judgment in default of defence and noting in default

division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.36(1)  Subject to subrule (2) and Part 11, Division 8, if a
defendant does not file a statement of defence or demand for
notice, or if the defendant’s statement of defence is struck out, the
plaintiff may, on filing an affidavit of service of the statement of
claim,
(a) enter judgment against the defendant under rule 3.38 or
3.39, or
(b) require the court clerk to enter in the court file of the
action, in Form 14, a note to the effect that the defendant
has not filed a statement of defence or demand for notice
and consequently is noted in default.
(2)  A judgment in default of filing a statement of defence must
not, without the Court’s permission, be entered against a person
who is represented by a litigation representative.
(3)  If the defendant has filed but has not served a statement of
defence or demand for notice, the plaintiff may apply to the Court
for a costs award against the defendant for anything arising from
the defendant’s failure.

BOOK_B.title: Judgment in default of defence and noting in default

commentary.text: Rule 3.36 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.36. 1. Effect of Noting in Default Noting in default is tantamount to an admission. The effect of [noting in default] is … to deem the allegations made to be proven. Klinck v. Drinnan (1985), 41 Alta. L.R. (2d) 299 (Q.B.), at 306, per Lutz J. Binder J. in Dykes v. Goczan (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 425 (Q.B.), noted one exception to the general rule that a defendant noted in default is deemed to have admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim. At pp. 426-27, his Lordship said: The effect of the Sulef decision [Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.)] which was approved by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith (1967), 60 W.W.R. 85, and applied by Lutz, J. in the Klinck case, is that when a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim by the failure to deny them. There is, however, an exception, which is the basis of the [Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.)] decision, that where the court is not satisfied that the plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter. In that case, for example, the trial judge had a suspicion that the plaintiff was manoeuvring to remove other defendants from the action to avoid the need to prove that the defendant who had not filed a defence was guilty of gross negligence. 2. Costs and Noting In Default In Capital One Bank v. Calhoun, 2007 ABQB 151, 2007 CarswellAlta 306, 427 A.R. 322, 75 Alta. L.R. (4th) 218, plaintiffs in a number of actions that were included in the application had noted the defendants in default, and were now seeking judgments which awarded solicitor-client costs for steps taken before and after judgment. The plaintiffs submitted that the defendants were deemed to have admitted the existence of agreements, the terms of which provided that the defendants had agreed to pay solicitor-client costs. Lee J. held that costs, being within the discretion of the Court, had to be determined by the Court. At pp. 221-222, his Lordship said: 13 Counsel for the Applicants seems to be submitting that the effect of noting the Defendant(s) in default results in his clients' entitlement to solicitor-client costs because the Statement of Claim says that the credit agreement provides for solicitor-client costs. The noting in default has the effect of deeming the facts plead as true, but I do not see it this way. … 15 The Applicants herein are entitled to their liquidated claims, namely the principal and interest owing on their credit card debts because the defendants were noted in default. 16 However, there is a difference between the Plaintiffs' entitlement to a liquidated demand, and the Plaintiffs' entitlement to solicitor-client costs. The principle amount claimed is admitted as part of the noting in default process, however costs are always the discretion of the Court, even in the face of a specific agreement between the parties; and regardless of an agreement, costs are always taxable. 17 While it may appear to be a simple proposition that the agreements provide for solicitor-client costs, a quick review for example of the Masters' various decisions with respect to mortgage foreclosures and solicitor-client costs certainly reveal that there is often much to argue about it in terms of the wording of agreements, and claims for solicitor and client costs. 18 Even if the wording in the agreement, and the claim fit the appropriate wording, there is still discretion in the Court to determine costs, and within that discretion, there is still the amount of costs to be determined. … 21 I am also in agreement with the present apparent practice of the Clerk of the Court not to tax post judgment costs on a solicitor-client basis, unless a Judge orders a specific award of solicitor-client costs. It is the Court, and not the Taxing Officers of the Court, that grant Judgments. The parties require the Court's approval for post judgment solicitor-client costs.
